title: Objective-C Quiz
description: Review the 12 starter lessons. The questions name the example to revisit. Take your time, use the lessons, and read the reason after each answer.

questions.question: printf is a C printing function. This Objective-C file can still use ordinary C code. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: printf uses the C part of the language. The pool surrounds any temporary Objective-C objects. Use a .m file so the compiler reads Objective-C.

questions.question: An int stores a whole number. %d tells printf where to place it. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: The int stores 3. The %d slot receives its sum with 2. Match the print format to the number type.

questions.question: NSString is an object holding text. The @ before the quotes makes an Objective-C string object. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: The @ literal makes an NSString. UTF8String gives printf a C string. Plain "Asha" is C text, not an NSString object.

questions.question: Square brackets send a message. length asks a string for its length in UTF-16 units. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: [word length] asks the NSString for its UTF-16 length. The three simple letters each use one unit. String length is not always the number of visible symbols.

questions.question: stringWithFormat makes text with inserted values. %@ inserts an object description. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: %@ inserts the name object into a new NSString. Its UTF-8 characters are printed. Use %@ for Objective-C objects, not %s.

questions.question: NSArray stores object values in order. The first index is zero. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: The array contains cat at zero and dog at one. Index 1 selects dog. Reading beyond the array count raises an exception.

questions.question: NSDictionary connects keys to values. A text key can describe the data. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: The title key selects its NSString. UTF8String reads that value for printing. Numbers in object collections need boxing such as @24.

questions.question: Objective-C keeps C if statements. The comparison produces a true-or-false result. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: The comparison is true, so the first printf is chosen. Use == for a numeric equality test, not assignment =.

questions.question: Fast enumeration visits each object in a collection using for-in. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: The loop receives each NSString in turn and prints its text. Do not change the collection while enumerating it.

questions.question: NSMutableArray allows changes such as adding an object. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: addObject adds a third object to the mutable array. count then gives 3. NSArray is read-only; use a mutable collection for changes.

questions.question: nil means no object. Checking it can select a fallback message. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: name is nil, so the conditional picks Guest. Do not add nil to an NSArray; it expects an object.

questions.question: isEqualToString compares string contents. Pointer equality asks whether two references point to one object. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: The second string joins c with at. Content equality finds the same letters in both strings. Use text equality when you care about the letters, not object identity.
